content: The Extensive Commentary on the Seven Points of the Noble Bhagavatī Mother Prajñāpāramitā Vajracchedikā.In the Indian language: Ārya-bhagavatī-prajñāpāramitā-vajracchedikā-sapta-dārtha-ṭīkā. In the Tibetan language: The Extensive Commentary on the Seven Points of the Noble Bhagavatī Mother Prajñāpāramitā Vajracchedikā. Homage to the Noble Prajñāpāramitā.To the peerless one who generates the qualities of the Buddhas,Who is the mother that nurtures the dharmadhātu,Who is the Vajracchedikā, difficult to divide, which accomplishes the benefit of others,And by holding which all noble ones are generated,Possessing the power of that which is designated merely by a name,Called the Vajra, the supreme among the pāramitās—Having heard the meaning of that which is taught by the speech of the one who taught it,I too shall strive to hold it.Because I also understand those meanings of it,I bow with the crown of my head to that which is the essence of all things.In order to grasp the meaning of the commentaries of others,I too have exerted myself in this explanation.This Prajñāpāramitā is established by setting forth seven points of meaning. These seven points of meaning are as follows: the uninterrupted lineage of the Buddhas, the nature of the application, its basis, the antidote, non-degeneration, the stages, and the reason for the title. Because these seven points of meaning serve as the basis for the Prajñāpāramitā, they are to be called points of meaning. It should be understood that the first six points of meaning fulfill the activities of a Bodhisattva, while the seventh fully demonstrates the purpose of this discourse on the Dharma.This Prajñāpāramitā also begins from the uninterrupted lineage of the Buddhas, for it explains how the lineage of the Buddhas becomes uninterrupted.The elder Subhūti himself, at the very beginning, elaborates on how wonderful it is that the Bhagavat Tathāgata has benefited the great Bodhisattvas in so many ways. Regarding this, "benefiting" refers to the ripening of Bodhisattvas at the time of attaining complete and perfect enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma, because it is for the sake of establishing Bodhisattvas in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through the five points of meaning. "Entrusting" refers to benefiting those who have not yet been ripened, for the sake of establishing them at the time of parinirvāṇa. Thus, by means of "benefiting" and "entrusting," the uninterrupted lineage is fully demonstrated.The characteristic of application is such as "how should a Bodhisattva abide?" and so forth. Regarding this, "abiding" is by way of aspiration and prayer. "Accomplishing" is by way of entering into meditative equipoise. "Holding the mind" is by way of suppressing distraction. Regarding this, aspiration is the intense desire, and prayer is the mental application of the mind toward the object that is intensely desired. Entering into meditative equipoise is whatever non-conceptual samādhi may be. Suppressing distraction is turning back from the praise of that which is not meditative equipoise and placing it in that very state. The first holds the path, the second completes the path, and the third demonstrates that the path does not degenerate.The basis for that is the very characteristic of application, and one should know that this basis also consists of eighteen aspects. These are: generating the mind of enlightenment; the application of the perfections; the aspiration to attain the form body; the aspiration to attain the dharma body; the absence of pride regarding the realization of the distinctions of meditation; the act of pleasing the arising of Buddhas; the prayer for the complete purity of the field; the maturing of sentient beings; being free from attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders; the application of being free from grasping at the bodies of sentient beings as a solid mass; worshipping and serving the Tathāgatas; being free from the acquisition and honors that have not been sought, by turning away from the exertion of wearying torment; the patience for suffering; being free from the taste of the flavor of samādhi; being free from the grasping of a "self" at the time of realization; seeking the instructions; realization; and seeking the Buddha-ground beyond that. These eighteen aspects are the basis upon which a Bodhisattva should abide, should accomplish, and should hold the mind.In order to liberate all sentient beings, one generates the mind of enlightenment, applies oneself to the perfections, and develops the aspiration to realize the Tathāgata’s form body or dharma body. By clearing away the obstacles to realization, one makes the mind completely detached, and by dispelling pride, one seeks the instructions for realization that make the mind completely detached for the sake of reaching the ultimate. From that, one achieves realization, and beyond that, one seeks the Buddha-ground; in this way, one should know the sequence of these various aspects. Regarding the generation of the mind, it is said, "A Bodhisattva should generate the mind in this way," and so forth. Regarding the application of the perfections, it is said, "A Bodhisattva should practice generosity without abiding in objects." Regarding the aspiration to attain the form body, it is said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be viewed by means of the perfection of marks?" and so forth. The dharma body is also of two types: the dharma body of teaching and the dharma body of realization. Regarding that, the dharma body of realization is also of two types: the nature of wisdom and the nature of merit.Regarding the aspiration to attain the dharma body of teaching, it is said, "Bhagavān, will there be sentient beings in the future time who will arise?" and so forth. The perception of the non-erroneous meaning should also be understood here as a correct perception; it is the perception that thinks "these are correct" due to being attached to a meaning that is not as the words state. Regarding the aspiration to attain the dharma body of the nature of wisdom, it is said, "Does the Tathāgata have any dharma by which he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?" and so forth. Regarding the aspiration to attain the dharma body of the nature of merit, it is said, "Whoever might take this trichiliocosm of great thousand worlds," and so forth. Regarding the absence of pride in having realized the distinction through meditation, it is said, "A stream-enterer thinks thus," and so forth. Regarding the act of pleasing the appearance of a Buddha, it is said, "Was there any dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, took from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara?" and so forth.Regarding the aspiration for the purification of the field, it is said, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva might say, 'I shall accomplish the adornments of the field,'" and so forth. Regarding the act of bringing sentient beings to full maturity, it is said, "Subhūti, it is like, for example, a person," and so forth. Regarding the detachment from attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders, it is said, "Subhūti, what do you think? As many grains of sand as there are in the river Ganges, are there that many rivers Ganges?" and so forth. Regarding the practice of being free from grasping at the body of a sentient being as a solid entity, it is said, "Again, Subhūti, if a son or daughter of noble family were to take as many grains of sand as there are in the trichiliocosm of great thousand worlds," and so forth. Regarding the act of making offerings and honoring the Tathāgata, it is said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, be viewed by means of the thirty-two marks of a great being?" and so forth. Regarding the turning away from exertion in weariness and torment, and the detachment from uninitiated gain and honor, it is said, "Again, Subhūti, if a man or woman were to abandon as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges," and so forth. Regarding this, weariness pertains to the body, and torment pertains to the mind; regarding the act of enduring suffering that is uninitiated, having turned away from exertion in those, it is said, "Again, Subhūti, what is the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom?" and so forth. Regarding the detachment from the enjoyment of the taste of meditative stabilization, it is said, "Again, Subhūti, if a man or woman were to [abandon] as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges," and so forth.With the intention of being free from the grasping of a "self" at the time of realization, the Blessed One spoke such words as, "How should a Bodhisattva abide?" With the intention of seeking the instructions, he spoke such words as, "Did the Tathāgata have any dharma by which he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara?" With the intention of realization, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, for example, if a person were possessed of a body and a great body," and so forth. Regarding that, "possessed of a body" means having attained a body, because one has attained the transformation of the basis that is the ultimate perfection of a complete body. "A great body" means because it takes up the bodies of all sentient beings. Beyond that, one should understand the seeking of the Buddha-ground, and that Buddha-ground is the transformation of the basis, which is comprised of six perfections. The six perfections are: the perfection of a purified field, the perfection of unsurpassed vision and primordial wisdom, the perfection of mastery over the heaps of merit, the perfection of the body, the perfection of speech, and the perfection of the mind.The perfection of the mind should be understood as the foundations of mindfulness, the perfect awakening, the designation as a dharma of great meaning, the designation as an instruction of great meaning, the complete inclusion of the dharmakāya, the non-abiding in nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, and the complete purity of movement and abiding. The complete purity of movement and abiding should be understood as the movement and abiding of conduct, the movement and abiding of mastery in the meditation on form and name, and the movement and abiding that are free from defilement. Freedom from defilement should be understood as freedom from defilement in the teacher and freedom from the defilement of saṃsāra. Regarding that, with the intention of the perfection of a purified field, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall accomplish the arrays of the fields,'" and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of unsurpassed vision, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?" and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of unsurpassed primordial wisdom, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? As many as are the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā," and so forth.With the intention of the perfection of the heap of merit, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? As for the world system of the great trichiliocosm," and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of the body of secondary marks, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be seen by the completion of the form body?" and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of the body of major marks, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be seen by the perfection of the marks?" and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of speech, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata think, 'I have taught the Dharma'?" and so forth. With the intention of the perfection of the mind as the foundations of mindfulness, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, those are neither sentient beings nor are they not sentient beings," and so forth. With the intention of the perfect awakening, he spoke such words as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?" and so forth. With the intention of the designation as a dharma of great meaning, he spoke such words as, "Furthermore, Subhūti, as many as are the kings of mountains, Mount Sumeru, in the world system of the great trichiliocosm," and so forth.With regard to establishing the instruction of the great meaning, he spoke such passages as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata think, 'I have liberated sentient beings'?" With regard to encompassing the dharmakāya, he spoke such passages as, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by the perfection of marks?" He said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by the perfection of marks as having fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?" And what is the further meaning? It is to clarify that enlightenment, which has the nature of the perfection of marks, also has the perfection of marks as its cause. With regard to not abiding in nirvāṇa, he spoke such passages as, "Again, Subhūti, do you think that those who have truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle destroy any dharma?" With regard to not abiding in saṃsāra, he spoke such passages as, "Subhūti, should a bodhisattva not grasp the heap of merit?" The statement "that which is to be grasped is not to be grasped, Subhūti" means that it is not to be grasped by the path; just as the heap of merit is, these also do not truly come into existence.With regard to the movement and abiding that are completely pure, being the movement and abiding of conduct, he spoke such passages as, "Does anyone go, Tathāgata?" With regard to the movement and abiding that are subject to the cultivation of form and name, he spoke such passages as, "Again, Subhūti, if a son or daughter of noble family were to take as many grains of sand as there are in the trichiliocosm..." With regard to the teacher who is free from the afflictions of saṃsāra in terms of movement and abiding, he spoke such passages as, "Again, Subhūti, as for a bodhisattva, the immeasurable and incalculable world-realms..." With regard to being free from the afflictions of saṃsāra, he spoke the verse:"Stars, darkness, a lamp,An illusion, dew, a bubble,A dream, lightning, and a cloud—View the conditioned thus."This verse teaches four characteristics of the conditioned: the characteristic of its essential nature, the characteristic of experiencing the taste of that which is not a basis for attachment, the characteristic of following after drawbacks, and the characteristic of following after definitive emergence.Regarding that, the characteristic of essential nature is consciousness, which is a view accompanied by marks. Regarding that, one should view marks as being like stars; for what reason? Because they appear in the darkness of ignorance, and because even if they exist in the light of wisdom, they go on to become invisible. One should view the view of a person and of phenomena as being like blurred vision; for what reason? Because it grasps at a meaning that has not become existent. One should view consciousness as being like a lamp; for what reason? Because it burns in dependence upon the fuel of grasping at craving. Regarding that, the characteristic of experiencing the taste of that which is not a basis for attachment is the experiencing of an object that is to be posited as erroneous; one should view that as being like an illusion; for what reason? Because it is an erroneous appearance. Regarding that, the characteristic of following after drawbacks is because it follows after impermanence, and also because it follows after suffering. Regarding that, by being like dew, the reality of the body being connected to moment-by-moment impermanence is made completely clear. By being like a bubble, the fact that feeling is connected to suffering is like a bubble. Having stated, "Whatever feeling there is, this is suffering here," feeling is suffering in accordance with the three types of suffering; regarding that, what arises from birth is the suffering of suffering itself.That which arises from separation is the suffering of change. That which arises from not being separated from correct association is the suffering of conditioned phenomena. Regarding that, even in the four dhyānas and the formless realms, it is established primarily by the feeling that is neither suffering nor happiness. Regarding that, the characteristic of following after renunciation is explained as the characteristic of renunciation, because by focusing on the non-self of persons and phenomena and following along with it, one renounces. Regarding that, following along also clarifies that conditioned phenomena such as the past are like dreams and so forth. Regarding that, past conditioned phenomena are like dreams because they reside in memory. The present is like a flash of lightning because it does not remain for a long duration. The future is like clouds because its seeds, through the latent propensity, cover the mind that is like the sky. Thus, because one fully understands the engagement of all conditioned phenomena of the three times, one should realize these as being without self; this is how the characteristic of following after renunciation is clearly taught. The supports for these are the supports that clarify the manifest similarities: the support of complete grasping, the support of the purification of pāramitā, the support of aspiration, the support of being devoid of obstacles, the support of purified intention, the support of finality, the support of vastness, and the support of profundity.The basis of upholding is the generation of bodhicitta. The basis of the purification of the pāramitās is the practice of the pāramitās. The basis of aspiration is the attainment of the rūpakāya and dharmakāya. The basis of being free from obstacles is the remaining twelve. The basis of the purification of intention is the realization. The basis of the ultimate is the seeking of the buddha-bhūmi beyond that. The basis of the vast and the profound is all of these. First, regarding the basis, the bodhisattva should generate bodhicitta, such as in the passage beginning with "Whatever beings there may be..." This is the vast, and the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva engages in the perception of a being..." is the profound, which is also the second basis. The passage beginning with "A bodhisattva should give a gift without abiding in objects..." and so forth is taught; this is the profound. The passage beginning with "Furthermore, the heap of merit of that one is not easy to measure..." and so forth is taught; this is the vast. In this way, one should understand the other bases as profound or vast as appropriate; the explanation of the bases is complete.What is the antidote? It should be understood as the antidote to two things: the characteristics of the practice of that [pāramitā] and the engagement with its basis. One practices incorrectly in two ways, including through the view of the transitory collection. Here, "view" when practicing correctly is intended as conceptualization. First, regarding the basis, the bodhisattva should generate bodhicitta in this way: the passage "Whatever beings there may be..." is the antidote to incorrect practice. Not generating the mind in that way becomes incorrect practice. The passage "If a bodhisattva engages in the perception of a being..." is the correct view, and thus the correct practice and the antidote. These are also things that are conceptually fixated upon, and the bodhisattva should abandon them. The second is the passage "I shall lead all beings to parinirvāṇa," and the passage "A bodhisattva should give a gift..." is the antidote to incorrect practice; if one does not give, the bodhisattva has entered into incorrect practice. The passage "A bodhisattva should give a gift without abiding in objects..." is the correct view, and thus the correct practice and the antidote. These are also things that are conceptually fixated upon, and the bodhisattva should abandon them and give the gift.What is non-degeneration? It is the complete abandonment of the two extremes. What are these extremes? They are the extreme of superimposition and the extreme of negation. The extreme of superimposition is the mental fixation upon phenomena as having an intrinsic nature that is not conceptualized, just as they appear in words. The extreme of negation is the mental fixation that there is no reality even upon the basis of the selflessness of phenomena. Regarding this, the passage "Bhagavān, that very heap of merit is not a heap" is what was spoken to negate the extreme of superimposition. Because that heap of merit does not exist, whatever exists just as it appears in words exists by way of a conceptualized intrinsic nature; therefore, the passage "The Tathāgata speaks of a 'heap of merit'" is what was spoken to negate the extreme of negation. That which is not an intrinsic nature as it appears in words exists to some slight degree, as it is an inexpressible reality, and the Tathāgata’s statement "a heap of merit" makes this fully clear. Likewise, the passage "Subhūti, the Buddha-qualities are not Buddha-qualities" negates the extreme of superimposition by stating that the Tathāgata speaks of those Buddha-qualities as non-existent, and the phrase "Buddha-qualities" negates the degeneration of the extreme of negation. Regarding this, the statement that the Tathāgata speaks of those Buddha-qualities as non-existent fully clarifies their unique meaning; therefore, the expression "Buddha-qualities" is appropriate to the meaning. If the Buddha-qualities did not exist by way of the intrinsic nature as described, then if the Tathāgata were to speak of them as non-existent, they would be understood as such even without the mention of "Buddha-qualities." Because their intrinsic nature does not exist, the Tathāgata spoke of "Buddha-qualities" for the sake of conventional designation. Likewise, one should understand this unique meaning to be appropriate to the meaning in all other cases as well. Here, one should understand the Buddha-qualities to be the perfections, the bases of social cohesion, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, as the factors of enlightenment. By this means, it should be stated that for those bodhisattvas, through the method of having completely abandoned the two extremes, there is no degeneration of the antidote.What are the stages? Here, the stages are considered to be of three types: the stage of engagement through aspiration, the stage of pure superior intention, and the stage of possessing the Tathāgata. Among these, the sixteen supports indicate the stage of engagement through aspiration, while the stage of pure superior intention is indicated by realization. The stage of possessing the Tathāgata is indicated by the complete search for the qualities of a Buddha.What is the reason for the title? The title "Vajracchedikā" should be understood in connection with two meanings, for it is said that through the authentic practice of this, one destroys views and defilements. It is called "vajra" because of its subtlety and essence; it is "subtle" because it is difficult to understand, and it is "essence" because it is difficult to abandon. Regarding this, it is the prajñāpāramitā that cuts through [these] by means of hearing, contemplation, and meditation. This is the vajra, this is the cutting, and the form of cutting completely is the Vajracchedikā. The vajra should be depicted as the two extremes being vast and the middle being condensed; because such a prajñāpāramitā is condensed into the middle, the stage of pure superior intention is fully indicated. By the beginning and the end being vast, the stage of engagement through aspiration and the stage of possessing the Tathāgata are fully indicated. Regarding this, the five points of meaning should be understood by relying authentically upon the subsequent ones; those stages are also the authentic support. The connection of the body of the sūtra has been explained.Now, the meaning of the words shall be expressed. If one asks, "For what reason did the Bhagavan abide in the deportment of a renunciant when teaching the Dharma?" it is to fully indicate the meaning that only a renunciant is capable of realizing this Dharma.Regarding the phrase "benefited by the holy one who provides benefit," what is the benefit provided to bodhisattvas? If one asks how it is "holy," the application of benefit and happiness is what constitutes "benefit provided," and one should understand it as "holy" by means of six causes: time, distinction, vastness, stability, pervasiveness, and category. As for time, how is it so? Because seeing the Dharma is itself the holy state. That, too, is the benefit provided to bodhisattvas, and because it is happiness itself, it is a state of seeing the Dharma. Because it is benefit itself, it is the state of the authentic beyond. As for distinction, how is it so? That is the worldly meditative absorption of those who are outsiders, whereas here, it is the supramundane meditative absorption, which is superior to the benefit provided to the noble śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. As for vastness, how is it so? Because the benefit provided is unsurpassable. As for stability, how is it so? Because it is the state of being extremely firm. How is it pervasive? Because it is the very act of providing benefit to one's own continuum and that of others. As for the category, how is it so? Because it is the most primary act of providing benefit to impure bodhisattvas. The holy one entrusts it completely. If one asks how the holy one does so, it is by means of six causes: through expansion, through specifically observing the dharmatā, through engaging in the knowledge of all, through non-decline, through compassion, and through the act of showing reverence.How is it that it is extensive? It is because of entrusting oneself completely to spiritual friends. How is it that one specifically focuses on the nature of phenomena? It is because those bodhisattvas who have been benefited generate the nature of phenomena that brings benefit to others. How is it that one engages in knowing all? It is because one makes it known to other bodhisattvas, saying, "These are the benefits that you have received." Through these three, one should understand what is meant by "not falling away," "possessing compassion," and "what is to be revered." For what reason did the elder Subhūti ask? It is for six reasons: the purpose of cutting off doubts, the purpose of engaging in superior aspiration, the purpose of following into the profound meaning, the purpose of what is not mistaken, the purpose of generating great joy, and the purpose of the holy Dharma remaining for a long time; thus, it is the prajñāpāramitā for the purpose of the lineage of the Tathāgata not being interrupted. In this regard, how is it that by these the lineage of the Buddha is not interrupted? It is for the purpose of cutting off the doubts of those who have doubts; for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas who desire merit but whose continuums are not yet mature to engage in superior aspiration toward the prajñāpāramitā by obtaining much merit; for the purpose of causing those whose continuums are mature to engage in the profound meaning; for the purpose of what is not mistaken, as those who have transformed obtain much merit by following those; for the purpose of genuinely generating joy in the very merit of realizing that Dharma, which is the essence for those whose superior intention of having benefited others is pure; and for the sake of the teaching of the Mahāyāna remaining for a long time in the future. In summary, it is for the purpose of correctly teaching those who have doubts, for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas who desire merit and are mature to correctly take it up, for the purpose of encouraging those who have transformed, and for the purpose of making those whose superior intention is pure genuinely joyful. Bodhisattvas are called sattva and mahāsattva because they are great due to seven types of greatness. What are the seven types of greatness? They are the greatness of Dharma, mind, aspiration, intention, accumulation, time, and all-pervading activity, according to the bodhisattva bhūmis.Why is this said? By stating "those who have truly entered the path of the Bodhisattva," it is the Elder Subhūti who has asked in the proper manner, as this is superior to the three types of enlightenment. By saying "having given approval, [I say] 'as many beings as are included in the category of beings,'" the general characteristic is indicated. By saying "those born from eggs, or..." and so forth, the specific characteristics are indicated; these should be understood through the distinctions mentioned regarding birth and abode. "Born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or miraculously born" refers to the distinctions of birth. "With form or without form" refers to the distinctions of abode. "With perception or without perception, or neither with perception nor without perception" refers to the distinctions of the object grasped. The statement "as many as are designated as the realm of beings" definitively indicates that the realm of beings in the state of those two types of characteristics is designated as a Buddha. The statement "all of them are to be led to parinirvāṇa" is a request for the meaning of how they are rendered incapable [of suffering]. Regarding "types," it is intended in terms of all types, such as those born from eggs and so forth as previously explained, and not in terms of number.Likewise, because those born from eggs, those born from moisture, those with perception, those without perception, and those neither with perception nor without perception are taken as the object, all beings must be led to parinirvāṇa by means of three causes: in order that those born in non-leisurely states may proceed to times of leisure, in order that those born in leisure who are not yet fully matured may be brought to maturity, and in order that those who are matured may be liberated. If one asks, "By what means?" it is stated as "into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder." This is precisely what is meant by "there is no parinirvāṇa." The Bhagavat also speaks of parinirvāṇa in terms of a sequence, for the purpose of abandoning the first dhyāna and so forth. That is the way in which the Buddhas train those to be tamed through the form of a reflected image, and it is also to be attained as the supreme state. Why is it that it is not stated as "into the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder"? That is a common fruit, for it is the fruit of one's own previous karma and the skillful means of the Buddhas. Even if it is not the ultimate in every respect, because it is from the pervasiveness of suffering for embodied beings, parinirvāṇa with remainder is the fruit of human effort, it is a common fruit, and it is the supreme state. It is explained as "without remainder" precisely because it is not the fruit of the ultimate supreme state.The statement, "Even though they have led immeasurable sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," indicates that the immeasurable nature of the various classes of beings, such as those born from eggs and so forth, is being fully demonstrated; the intention is that not a single sentient being is actually led to nirvāṇa. Regarding the statement, "If a bodhisattva were to think that they themselves have led them to complete nirvāṇa, then there would be no such thing," what is the reasoning? If a bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being, they should not be called a bodhisattva. What is the intention here? If a bodhisattva engages in the perception of sentient beings as something other than themselves, they are engaging in the perception of a self, and therefore they should not be called a bodhisattva. And what is the intention behind the statement, "engaging in the perception of a sentient being, or the perception of a life-principle, or the perception of a person"? It is that for one who engages in the perception of grasping at sentient beings, life-principles, and persons—which are characterized by defilement—they also engage in the perception of a self regarding the self, and they engage in the perception of sentient beings regarding sentient beings. However, for a bodhisattva, because they have abandoned the view of a self, these perceptions do not occur. Therefore, because the characteristics of conditioned phenomena are identical, the bodhisattva who has the conviction that self and others are equal is not one who holds the view of grasping at sentient beings, life-principles, or persons; this is the intention of this passage."One should not generate the mind in such a way"—by this, it is fully shown how a bodhisattva should abide through aspiration and prayer."If a bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being, they should not be called a bodhisattva"—by this, it is fully shown how one should accomplish [the path] at the time of being in meditative equipoise."If one engages in the perception of a sentient being, or engages in the perception of a life-force, or engages in the perception of a person, they should not be called a bodhisattva"—by this, it is fully shown how one should firmly hold the mind at the time of subduing distraction. When a bodhisattva does not engage in the perception of a sentient being at the time of entering into meditative equipoise or at the time of subduing distraction, that is the occasion to be known by such characteristics. Therefore, the thought that "not even one sentient being will attain parinirvāṇa" is a dualistic way of thinking that should not be entertained.The aspiration and prayer and so forth that have already been explained are the characteristics of engaging in the support of what is to be fully grasped. Because it is certain that in other supports, one will emerge by relying on that very aspiration and prayer, the aspiration and prayer and so forth are explained again in detail. From these, one should understand that the way of engaging in those aforementioned supports is explained through five aspects: the degeneration of meaning, the mere sign being widely known, the clarifying, the establishing, and the seeing correctly. The degeneration of meaning is the adverse factor of the support. The mere sign of that very support is from what is widely known. The clarifying is through aspiration and prayer. The establishing is through the ultimate meaning. The seeing correctly is through entering into meditative equipoise and subduing distraction.In that regard, concerning the support of the purified prajñāpāramitā, the statement that "a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding in things" is made; the degeneration of its meaning is stated to be the adverse factor of abiding itself. The statement "gives a gift" is from what is widely known as the mere sign.Here, the six pāramitās are summarized by taking the nature of generosity as the basis for the three types of generosity. Through the generosity of material goods, there is the pāramitā of generosity. Through the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of ethical discipline and the pāramitā of patience. Through the generosity of the Dharma, there is the pāramitā of diligence, the pāramitā of meditative concentration, and the pāramitā of wisdom; for without diligence, one would not teach the Dharma while weary of grasping and teaching it. Without meditative concentration, one would not endure cold and heat due to the desire to be mastered by faith, and would manifest as completely afflicted. Without wisdom, one would teach in a distorted way, and it is said, "from what would one degenerate?" If these three are not absent, the generosity of the Dharma is perfect. These pāramitās also have two types of results: those of the future life and those of the visible life. Through the pāramitā of generosity, the result of the future life is great enjoyment. Through the pāramitā of ethical discipline, there is the perfection of the body, such as being Śakra or Brahmā. Through the pāramitā of patience, there is having a large faction and a large retinue. Through the pāramitā of diligence, there is the continuity of enjoyment and so forth. Through the pāramitā of meditative concentration, one achieves non-harmfulness. Through the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and pleasant, there is much mental happiness, and one gains mastery over a great assembly of beings. As for the visible life, there is supreme faith in all things and nirvāṇa in the visible life. In that regard, if a bodhisattva, while seeking the result of future generosity, gives a gift, that is generosity that abides in things, because it abides in the thing to be given and in the thing that is such a result.Therefore, it is stated that one should practice generosity without abiding in objects.Alternatively, if one practices generosity while seeking the results of ethical discipline and so forth, it is a practice of generosity that abides in something; therefore, it is stated that one should practice generosity without abiding in anything at all. The term "anything at all" is used because there is no distinction in the multiplicity of the results of ethical discipline and so forth.Alternatively, if one practices generosity while seeking the results of the visible world that are governed by faith, it is a practice of generosity that abides in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile sensations; therefore, it is stated that one should practice generosity without abiding in forms, and so forth. Alternatively, if one practices generosity while seeking nirvāṇa in the visible world, it is a practice of generosity that abides in phenomena; therefore, it is stated that one should practice generosity without abiding in phenomena. The instruction that one should practice generosity indicates the aspiration and prayer for generosity. The instruction that one should practice generosity without abiding in anything is the establishment of the ultimate truth.In this regard, the state of not abiding clarifies the ultimate truth that is to be meditated upon just as it is, while the state of not abiding in objects and so forth is the very extent of what is to be meditated upon. This is the meaning of the statement that a bodhisattva should practice generosity without abiding in the perception of characteristics. The term "not abiding" indicates the overcoming of distraction for one who has entered into meditative equipoise; at that time, one does not abide in the perception of characteristics.In this way, for a bodhisattva who is engaging in non-abiding, whether they lack enthusiasm due to dependence on merit or are seeking it through enthusiasm, the great mass of merit from practicing generosity without abiding is fully demonstrated, and it is comparable to space in three ways. It is comparable to space because, through its all-pervading nature, it is consistent with the arising of merit whether one is abiding or not abiding. It is comparable to space because, through its vastness, it is a supreme distinction. It is comparable to space because, through its inexhaustibility, it is a boundless generosity.Regarding the passage, "Again, Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be viewed by means of the perfection of marks?"—this shows that, because the meaning is lost, the pride of viewing the Tathāgata in terms of a physical body is a discordant factor. If one asks what kind of spiritual friend one must be fully seized by, the elder Subhūti replied, "No, Bhagavan." The Blessed One then elaborated, "Subhūti, to the extent that there is a perfection of marks, to that extent it is false." By this, he refers to aspiration and prayer.The meaning here is to demonstrate the establishment of the ultimate truth; for in the ultimate sense, the perfection of marks is false, whereas the absence of the perfection of marks is not false.The statement, "In this way, the Tathāgata should be viewed as having marks and as being without marks," correctly demonstrates the overcoming of distraction for one who has entered into meditative equipoise; at that time, one should view the marks as being precisely the absence of marks.Regarding the basis of aspiring to attain the taught dharmakāya, the passage "Will there be any sentient beings who will generate such a perception..." refers to those who [will generate] such a perception regarding the final words of the sūtra. One should understand the "words of the sūtra" here as referring to those that are about to be explained. If one asks what kind of words these are, they are those that have been spoken as the words of the seven meanings. The elder Subhūti [speaks of] the arising of those bodhisattvas who will generate such a perception in the future time. Having negated that which will not arise, the Bhagavan states that they will arise; one should also understand that the destruction of dharmas is the complete loss of practice. If one asks what kind of practice is [being discussed] in those [passages], it is because the mere cause of the perfection of marks has been proclaimed, through which the rūpakāya of the Tathāgata is fully demonstrated, which connects to the phrase "by having grasped the merit." The Bhagavan has fully demonstrated how, by means of a correct perception, one who possesses such a perception will arise.The phrases "possessing ethical conduct," "possessing qualities," and "possessing wisdom" fully demonstrate the practice of the three trainings, beginning with the higher ethical conduct. The mention of "qualities" refers to the meditative absorption that is preceded by qualities such as having few desires. The statement "they will perform service to many hundreds of thousands of buddhas" is a proclamation of the extensive causes that will arise. The phrase "having a mind that is completely pure in a single way" refers to those who, among those previously explained, are the first to generate such a perception of arising. The statement "the Tathāgata knows them" means that the Tathāgata knows their names, bodies, consciousnesses, and views.By relying on the knowledge of the thought that "all that remains and moves is seen through the vision of the rūpakāya," the views are indicated; these indicate being sustained by a spiritual friend, and the phrase "an immeasurable mass of merit" indicates being sustained by merit. One desires to be sustained at the time of practicing and generating merit, because at the time of its cessation, one is sustaining the seed.The statement "those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of a sentient being, up to the point that if they were to engage in the perception of the non-existence of phenomena, that very thing would become their grasping at a self" indicates their correct perception. This is the antidote to five types of erroneous grasping. What are these five types of erroneous grasping? They are the perceptions of others—such as tīrthikas, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas who possess pride, and those who fall into the perception of worldly commonality—or those who fall into the perception of non-perception. The first involves engaging in the perception of a self; the second involves the perception of phenomena; the third involves the perception of non-phenomena, for because they perceive phenomena as substantial, the non-existence of the substantiality of phenomena is here considered to be "non-phenomena." The fourth is engaging in the perception of [a self], and the fifth is the perception of non-perception. Those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of any of these. Therefore, it is taught that "they will possess ethical conduct," up to the point that "they will possess an immeasurable mass of merit."Because it is stated, "For what reason?", it is because whatever erroneous grasping occurs is the engaging in the perception of phenomena and the perception of non-phenomena. That which is the non-engagement of the perception of selflessness and so forth is also a perception of a self and so forth; because those latent tendencies have not been abandoned, this very thing becomes grasping at a self. Therefore, if those bodhisattvas engage in the perception of phenomena, that very thing becomes their grasping at a self. By stating "if they engage in the perception of non-phenomena," it is taught that the remaining ones also engage in the perception of a self and so forth.Even if the word "itself" is not stated, it means that this very thing becomes their grasping at a self. In this regard, the grasping that determines [something] as one's own continuum is to be understood as the perception of a self, and the grasping at the existence of what is "mine" is the perception of a sentient being. The grasping at a self as enduring for as long as life lasts is the perception of a life force. The grasping at going into the realms of rebirth again and again is the perception of a person. It is said that for those, one should generate the correct perception. Regarding the words of the sūtra that will be explained, the incorrect perception of the meaning being lost is shown to be the adverse factor, whereas by merely stating the cause, the Dharmakāya that is taught is fully revealed.The statement "generate the correct perception" indicates the aspiration and prayer for generating that [perception]. The statement "their grasping at a self will not occur" sets forth the ultimate meaning in detail. Furthermore, the statement "Subhūti, one should not grasp at a dharma, nor at what is not a dharma" indicates the cutting off of the distraction of one who has entered into meditative equipoise; the meaning is that at that time, both grasping at what is not a dharma and grasping at what is not "not a dharma" are conceptualizations regarding the selflessness of phenomena. That is the Dharmakāya that is taught. Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke this for the sake of sentient beings.For those who understand the discourse on the Dharma as being like a raft, even the Dharma is to be abandoned; thus, it is taught that before generating the correct perception, what is not a dharma—these things—are taught. In summary, it is fully taught that a Bodhisattva should aspire to attain the Dharmakāya that is taught by the correct perception.The basis for the aspiration to attain the Dharmakāya, which is the realization of the nature of primordial wisdom, is: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?" By this, he indicates that to grasp at an awakening that is to be realized, based on the degeneration of the meaning, is a discordant factor; it is said that by teaching the Dharma, one grasps at that as perfect awakening. Therefore, he said, "Is there any dharma that has been taught?"—namely, what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. By merely expressing the cause, the Dharmakāya of realization is taught. By saying "No," the Elder Subhūti expressed the Buddha’s intention, indicating an aspiration and prayer that is free from grasping at awakening in a conventional sense; he intended that, in terms of the discourse, both of these exist. The Blessed One’s statement indicates that, in that sense, neither of these exists."As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said," he says. Why is this? It is because of what the Tathāgata said when he asked, "What is the dharma that the Tathāgata has taught?""Not to be grasped and not to be expressed; it is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma"—by this, he establishes the ultimate, for the sake of realizing the taught dharma, which is awakening. He establishes the ultimate by taking the nature of phenomena as the basis; in this context, "not to be grasped" means it cannot be listened to. "Not to be expressed" means there is no dharma that is the very thing taught, and because of the selflessness of phenomena, there is also no non-dharma in terms of the nature of the imagined."Why is this?" The statement "Noble beings are distinguished by the unconditioned" means that they do not conceptualize in terms of conditioned phenomena; by this, the bodhisattva who is a learner is distinguished. "Unborn" means that although it exists, it is unconditioned, and because the transformation of the Tathāgata's state is distinguished by the purity of suchness, by this, the Tathāgata who is a non-learner is distinguished. In this context, the first meaning of "unconditioned" indicates entering into meditative equipoise, and it also indicates the subduing of distraction therein. The second meaning indicates the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, which has the meaning of the perfection of wisdom. From this, one should understand that all higher supports are distinguished by the unconditioned, as this is said with the noble beings in mind. Because the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is taught here without having previously spoken of being distinguished by the unconditioned, the unconditioned is attained by way of its meaning. If one asks what is being fully taught regarding the support of the dharmakāya that realizes the nature of merit, it is because the dharmakāya that is realized from the Tathāgatas—who have a nature endowed with merit—arises from the dharmakāya that is taught for the time being. That is also how the teaching of the four-line verse is to be understood for the time being. The source of great merit is, in the first instance, this dharmakāya that is realized by the Tathāgatas, which is the nature of merit.Furthermore, what is the reason for this? If one were to teach even a single four-line stanza from the Dharma body that has been taught, such merit would become vast.Why is that? It is because the statement, "The unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgatas arises from this," is taught as a demonstration, for it is understood by relying upon the brief teaching of the ten practices.The statement, "The Buddha Blessed Ones are born from this," refers to the conventional Buddha, because enlightenment arises from that. For both, the quality of the Buddha is the stūpa. That very enlightenment is the Buddha.Therefore, Subhūti, the statement "Buddha-dharmas, Buddha-dharmas" is taught as "the absence of those Buddha-dharmas." In this regard, this is to be understood for the time being as the cause for the arising of much merit; however, by the falling away of the meaning, it is fully taught that the opposing side of merit arises abundantly. By merely expressing the cause called "merit," the Dharmakāya, which is the nature of merit, is fully taught. By the very teaching of supreme merit, one also demonstrates the aspiration for it: "Bhagavān, that very mass of merit is a non-mass, and therefore the Tathāgata has spoken of it as a 'mass of merit'.""Subhūti, the statement 'Buddha-dharmas, Buddha-dharmas' is taught as 'the absence of those Buddha-dharmas,' and therefore they are called 'Buddha-dharmas.' By this, the mass of merit that was spoken of is also addressed; for whoever fully grasps the Buddha-dharmas, the Dharmakāya, which is the nature of merit, is established in the ultimate sense, based on the fact that it belongs to those Tathāgatas. This is a further teaching to cut off the distraction of one who has entered into meditative equipoise, following the instruction that 'noble beings are distinguished by the unconditioned.' 'Bhagavān, it is much; Sugata, it is much'—the utterance of these two phrases indicates that it is grasped as a self-nature, and thus it points to a self-nature that is grasped as a self; it is taught as taking hold of what is grasped as superior, which is the meaning of the statement 'it should be taught by words and letters.' 'Immeasurable' means it is not an object of analogy, and 'countless' means it is vast. This is the basis of aspiration. The basis of being free from obstacles should be understood as the antidote to the twelve obstacles. What are the twelve obstacles? They are: having manifest pride; even if one is without manifest pride, having little learning; even if one has much learning, practicing only minor mental engagement; even if one’s mental engagement is not minor, abandoning sentient beings; even if one does not abandon them, being attached to external treatises; even if one does not engage in those, being unskilled in suppressing the signs of illusions; even if one is skilled in that, not accumulating the collection of merit; even if one accumulates the collection of merit, being overcome by laziness and tasting the flavor of the happiness of honor and respect; even if one does not taste that flavor, being unable to endure suffering; even if one can endure suffering, not accumulating the collection of wisdom; and even if one accumulates the collection of wisdom, holding to a self, or even if one does not hold to a self, being devoid of oral instructions.In order to emphasize the state of being free from overweening pride, the passage "A srota-āpanna thinks thus" was spoken at length. In this context, the failure of meaning—that is, the state of having overweening pride by thinking "I have attained"—is indicated as the discordant factor.By the phrase "A srota-āpanna thinks thus," the absence of overweening pride is fully demonstrated simply by stating the cause, and through this, aspiration and prayer are also indicated. By the phrase "Blessed One, he does not enter into anything at all," the ultimate truth is established.If a srota-āpanna were to think, "I have attained the fruit of a srota-āpanna," that itself would be his grasping at a self. Therefore, it should be understood that this becomes his overweening pride. This applies likewise up to the level of an arhat. The meaning to be grasped by these words is that, through the distinction of the Sthavira Subhūti, one realizes and directly perceives the qualities of an arhat, which are common to both dwelling and moving. Just as it is said that for an arhat there is no entering into anything at all, so too it is said that there is no dwelling in anything at all; thus, the ultimate truth of dwelling and moving is established here as well.In order to emphasize the state of being free from having heard little, the Tathāgata asked, "Was there any dharma that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara obtained?" By this, attachment to the arising of a Buddha is indicated; therefore, by stating "any dharma obtained," conceptual proliferation is abandoned. The failure of meaning is due to the application of the practice to discordant factors and the like.In order to emphasize the state of being free from the meditation of minor mental engagement with objects, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall accomplish the arrays of the buddha-fields'..." When one mentally engages with the arrays of the fields, one tastes the flavor of that which is based on the conceptualization of form and the like.For the purpose of completely abandoning that, [it is said]: "Subhūti, therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of awakening in this way, by not dwelling."This is what is explained at length by the words, "by not dwelling in anything at all."In order to emphasize the state of being free from abandoning sentient beings, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body were to become like this..." What is shown by this? It refers to those who delight in the complete maturation of sentient beings in the desire realm. Regarding that, the size of the body of the asura-king Rāhu is equal to Mount Meru, and even that is to be viewed as temporarily lacking a body; what need is there to mention others?The statement "The Tathāgata has spoken of the absence of entities" indicates the selflessness of phenomena as suchness. To say "there are no entities" is to point completely to the suchness that is non-arisen and unconditioned. This is to point completely to the selflessness of phenomena in terms of their intrinsic nature and their specific characteristics.In order to emphasize the state of being free from attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? As many as are the grains of sand in the river Ganges..." Here, four causes are used to point completely to the excellence of this Dharma: the accumulation of merit, being honored by many such as gods, the cause of performing hardships, and being contemplated and accompanied by the Tathāgata and others.The statement "This is the cause for generating much merit from this" refers to the accumulation of merit. The statement "That place of earth becomes a stūpa" refers to being honored by many such as gods.The statement "It will be endowed with supreme wonder" refers to the cause of performing hardships.The statement "The Teacher also abides in that place, and other places of the Guru also abide" refers to being contemplated and accompanied by the Tathāgata and others. Regarding this, it is said "to be taught by way of what has been spoken and what will be spoken, and by way of the Teacher." By thoroughly pointing out the excellence of this Dharma as an antidote to attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders, one should not become attached to this very Dharma as if it were merely the literal words; rather, it serves as an antidote to the future faults of those [treatises].The statement "That which the Tathāgata has spoken as the prajñāpāramitā is not a pāramitā" means that just as the prajñāpāramitā is not a pāramitā, in the same way, the Tathāgata has not taught any Dharma at all; this is the meaning being thoroughly pointed out. It is said "what the Tathāgata has spoken as Dharma," and this discourse on Dharma thoroughly points out the ultimate reality through its own and general characteristics.Because those who are unskilled in suppressing the signs of images are in need of being led away from them, it is explained at length: "Subhūti, as for the number of atoms of earth in the great trichiliocosm world system..." This is because Bodhisattvas who contemplate great objects will extensively cultivate the mental engagement of focusing on world systems; therefore, the great trichiliocosm world system is mentioned.In this regard, two methods are taught for the purpose of suppressing the signs of the images of the rūpakāya. The method for making them subtle is what is stated: "Is the number of atoms of earth in the great trichiliocosm world system many?"The method for making them appear as non-existent is because the Tathāgata has spoken of those that are atoms of earth as being without atoms; therefore, it is stated: "That is why they are called atoms of earth."For the purpose of suppressing the signs of the images of the body, the Tathāgata has taught that the world system is without a world system; therefore, it is stated: "That is why it is called a world system." Here, "world system" is intended as the world of sentient beings, and the statement that "what is distinguished by name and form is the world of sentient beings" is the skill in the method of making them appear as non-existent. In this regard, the purpose of suppressing the signs of the images is fully taught, but it is not a method for making them subtle.With regard to those who are devoid of having accumulated the collection of merit, it is stated: "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened Buddha be viewed by means of the thirty-two marks of a great person?" What is taught by this? It is that while the Tathāgata should be worshipped and served for the sake of the collection of merit, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the perfect marks; rather, one should view him by means of the ultimate reality of the Dharma.With regard to those who are devoid of having tasted the bliss of laziness, gain, and honor, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what if a man or woman were to give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges?" What is taught by this? It is that while the merit from giving away bodies for a time is indeed that much, one should not be interrupted by the laziness that relies upon a single body for as long as one exists.Why does the Elder Subhūti shed tears? It is stated: "Since I have attained wisdom, I have not heard such a discourse on the Dharma." Although I have heard that giving away a great many bodies results in great and supreme merit, this is not teaching that merit is supreme here; rather, having heard that merit becomes supreme in that way, one initiates diligence and develops a perception of the Dharma just as it is.In order to abandon the faults of those, it is stated: "Those who will generate a correct perception when this sūtra is taught will be endowed with supreme wonder."Regarding this, the statement "Whatever is 'correct perception' is 'no perception'" is explained at length in order to abandon the conceptualization of correct perception, which is what "correct perception" is.The passage "Blessed One, I am not amazed" is also explained at length. What is the meaning? It is to gather those future bodhisattvas who have become lazy due to the faults of tasting the bliss of gain and honor into a state of shame. For the sake of those bodhisattvas who will appear at the time when the sublime Dharma is disintegrating, this discourse on the Dharma will be taken up, and they will not grasp at them as persons, nor as phenomena.When you are celebrating the feast of the sublime Dharma, because there is no attainment, it brings one to a state of shame; it teaches that they will not engage in the perception of a self, and it teaches that they will not grasp at a person.The statement "Whatever is 'perception of a self' is 'no perception'" teaches that there is no grasping at phenomena.As for the reason why, the statement "Because the Tathāgata Buddhas are free from all perceptions" points to those bodhisattvas who are training accordingly; it means that since the Tathāgata Buddhas are free from all perceptions, we too must train in that same way. In this context, the intention of the explanation is that, having taken as the basis the state of being free from the reversal of diligence, one who possesses a continuum free of conceptualization will be liberated. "Will be taken up" refers to the literal text, while "will be fully understood" refers to the meaning.Based on the state of being free from non-exertion, it is explained in detail that "in this regard, one will not be afraid when the words of the sūtra are explained." Fear is the failure to initiate diligence. The Bhagavat has taught that for the Śrāvaka vehicle, there is the emptiness of phenomena alone, whereas for the Mahāyāna, it is taught that neither exists by way of an imputed nature. Upon hearing this, one becomes afraid when hearing that phenomena do not exist, and one becomes terrified when hearing that emptiness is without substantiality; and when one contemplates that because both are without substantiality, one is unable to apply or engage in them, one becomes completely terrified. Furthermore, one should understand this as a series of synonyms based on the three types of lack of intrinsic nature: the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics, and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate.Why is that? Regarding the statement, "Subhūti, this supreme prajñāpāramitā has been spoken by the Tathāgata," what is the meaning? It establishes the second basis of shame, meaning that because this teaching is paramount, one should be conscientious. In this regard, the other pāramitās are pāramitās only because of this paramount nature.The statement "the supreme prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgata has spoken" is taught by the phrase "immeasurable buddhas," which indicates that because this prajñāpāramitā has been spoken by all buddhas as well, it should be called "supreme."In terms of being free from the inability to endure suffering, the Tathāgata has further spoken at length, "Subhūti, the Tathāgata’s kṣānti-pāramitā." Regarding this, by what signs can one know that kṣānti which has been spoken of? What is the nature of kṣānti? What is the cause and the antidote of kṣānti? I shall state it: the teaching that kṣānti is just as it is through the individual realization of the selflessness of phenomena is what is meant by the statement, "That which is the Tathāgata’s kṣānti-pāramitā is itself not a pāramitā." By what sign should one recognize kṣānti? If, while being harmed, one does not have the perception of a malicious mind arising from the basis of the perception of a self and so forth, that is it. One does not perceive this as being the kṣānti-pāramitā, nor does one perceive it as not being a pāramitā; thus, its nature is taught.It is stated at length, "When the King of Kalinga severed my limbs and appendages, at that time I had no perception of a self." Regarding this, how is it that one endures in such a manner? It is to fully demonstrate how one endures intense suffering and also endures continuous suffering, which is why it is stated, "When the King of Kalinga severed my limbs and appendages."The statement, "Also, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi called Kṣāntivādin," refers to the causes of patience, which are the three types of suffering: the suffering of saṃsāra, the suffering of being harmed by sentient beings, and the suffering of being deprived of resources.Regarding that, the statement, "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by completely abandoning all perceptions," is a teaching on the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of saṃsāra. There are three types of generating the mind for enlightenment: it is the unwillingness to generate it due to the perception of suffering; therefore, it is stated at length, "by completely abandoning all perceptions." Here, there are three types: the perception of suffering, all perceptions of desiring to dwell in form and so forth, and the mind not generating enlightenment because it is completely exhausted by these sufferings of saṃsāra.The statement, "One should generate the mind without dwelling in form," is as described before.Likewise, the statement, "One should not abide in phenomena, nor should one abide in non-phenomena," means that one should not abide in phenomena, nor should one abide in the selflessness of phenomena. The state of not abiding in them is explained at length as follows: because that which is "abiding" is itself non-abiding, in order to refute the conceptualization of an intrinsic nature that corresponds literally to the words used here.Furthermore, the statement, "A bodhisattva should completely give away gifts for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings," and the explanation at length, "Whatever perception of sentient beings there is, that itself is also a non-perception," fully demonstrate the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of being harmed by sentient beings; it is said that one gives away everything for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. Since those sentient beings—to whom one is attached, thinking, "I am the agent and this is the action"—do not exist, from what cause could there be a perception of sentient beings that would produce weariness toward the wrong practices of sentient beings? Thus, it also fully demonstrates the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.Subhūti, what is being taught by the extensive statement, "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth"? It means that one should also endure through having genuine faith in the Tathāgata. In this regard, "one who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of conventional truth. "One who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified. "This" refers to the truth of the practice, which is to say, "one should be thoroughly afflicted and one should be completely purified."It is in terms of the characteristics of ultimate truth that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness." It is in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness" and as "one who speaks the truth." Here, "truth" refers to the fact that, in order to completely abandon the clinging to a literal essence, the Tathāgata has stated that for any phenomenon that he has fully awakened to or taught, there is neither truth nor falsehood. There is no truth because it is devoid of a literal essence; there is no falsehood because it exists as a non-literal essence.Subhūti, the extensive statement, "It is like a person who has entered the darkness," fully demonstrates the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of lacking material resources. Whoever gives gifts for the sake of material resources is giving gifts while falling into the perception of entities, and that falling is for the sake of desiring happiness and being free from suffering.Feelings do not generate a definitive renunciation; just as one who has entered the darkness thinks, "How can I proceed?" and therefore delights in the pleasure of desire, the one who gives gifts without falling into the perception of entities is like a person with sight at daybreak, when the sun has risen and diverse forms are seen, who looks, thinking, "How shall I proceed?" That person, having passed the night of ignorance and with the sun of wisdom having risen, generates the vision of diverse knowable objects exactly as they are. Otherwise, one would not delight in the pleasure of desire, for there is a definitive renunciation from the feelings of pleasure and pain of desire.In order to address the lack of the accumulation of wisdom, it is said, "Subhūti, any son or daughter of good family who takes up this discourse on the Dharma," and so forth. Here, for the sake of those who are devoid of tasting the flavor of samādhi, five distinct qualities of what is called the yoga of Dharma are demonstrated: being kept in mind and accompanied by the Tathāgata, the complete acquisition of merit, praise for practicing the Dharma, being honored by gods and others, and the exhaustion of negative deeds. What is meant by being kept in mind and accompanied by the Tathāgata? It is what was said: "The Tathāgata knows them; the Tathāgata beholds them."Regarding that, it is what was said: "taking up, reading, retaining, not forgetting, speaking, and mastering." This refers to taking up the cause of the dhāraṇī of retention, and the desire to read, retain, and master. Furthermore, "speaking, reading, and mastering" refers to retaining the meaning. If you ask how merit is completely acquired, it is what was said: "All those sentient beings will generate an immeasurable heap of merit." It is also explained at length that they will not forget.If you ask how this is praise for practicing the Dharma, it is what was said at length: "Subhūti, this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and incomparable."The praise of the Dharma is this: "inconceivable" means it is to be realized by each person individually; "incomparable" means it is because there is no distinction of equality.This discourse on the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, which is called the aim of sentient beings who have truly entered the supreme vehicle, establishes the very state of being incomparable.Regarding that, in comparison to other vehicles, it should be known as supreme and known as primary because it completely purifies the obscurations of defilement and the obscurations of knowledge. As it is said, "The Tathāgata sees those who take up this discourse on the Dharma, from taking it up to mastering it." This and those [statements] are praise for the practice, as it is explained at length: "All those sentient beings will possess immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, incalculable, and limitless [merit]."All of them will have my awakening placed upon their shoulders; they will increase the burden of awakening. Subhūti, this discourse on the Dharma cannot be heard by those who are inclined toward the inferior, namely those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.The statement "not those who have a view of a self" is an explanation of Bodhisattvas who have a view of a person.What is meant by being honored by gods and others? It is as the Tathāgata explained at length: "Subhūti, any place on earth where this sūtra is taught is worthy of worship," and so forth. Regarding that, it means making offerings with flowers, incense, parasols, victory banners, flags, and so forth, as well as bowing down, paying homage, circumambulating, offering alms, and [making it a place] that becomes a stūpa. What is meant by the exhaustion of negative deeds? It is that these [negative deeds] will be completely worn away.In order to fully demonstrate the many ways in which they are completely worn away, it is stated that they will be "extremely worn away," that the awakening of a Buddha will also be attained, and that obscurations and negative deeds will be completely exhausted. Therefore, it is also said that, furthermore, they will emerge from falling [into lower realms], and that extremely numerous, immeasurable, and innumerable merits will arise. It should be understood that this is an explanation of "immeasurable" and "innumerable," because it is also the case that extreme suffering will arise and that a great multitude will arise.Regarding that, the statement "Subhūti, I cognize the immeasurable and even more immeasurable eons," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates that which is supreme. This is the arising of the heap of merit of this [sūtra], and that heap of merit is supreme and surpasses all others. Regarding that, it should be understood that for as long as the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara existed, it was for immeasurable eons; the statement that "by that, one has pleased [the Buddhas] in ways that are even more immeasurable" is a summary. "Not having produced a thought" means being without pride.Furthermore, the statement "Subhūti, if I were to describe the heap of merit of those sons or daughters of noble family," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates a great multitude. Regarding that, it should be understood that the "myo myo po" (the confused state) is the cause, and the "disturbed mind" is the result.Now, if one asks how the arising of merit is, the statement "Subhūti, this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable, and its ripening is also inconceivable," indicates that this completely demonstrates that the fruit of merit does not depend upon logical reasoning.The statement "How," and so forth, as explained at length, is spoken in the context of being free from grasping at a self, having truly entered into the Bodhisattva vehicle. If one asks why that is, it demonstrates the initial question itself: one should view the Bodhisattva who is abiding beyond the limit of realization as understanding the distinctiveness of the self, saying, "I am abiding in that." By practicing in that way, "I shall thus firmly hold the mind." The statement "Now I shall cause sentient beings to attain complete nirvāṇa," and so forth, is the elaboration.As an antidote to that, there is abiding in that, and also how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should firmly hold the mind.Once this was requested, the Bhagavat gave a prediction. The elaboration, "How should one generate the mind?" and the statement, "I shall cause sentient beings to attain complete nirvāṇa, yet there is no sentient being who has attained complete nirvāṇa," are spoken as an antidote to grasping at a self.The statement, "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being," is intended to mean that this arises from grasping at correctness or from latent tendencies. The statement, "Abiding in the vehicle of the Bodhisattva of perfect, complete enlightenment," is spoken as an antidote to grasping at a self.It is also because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that can be called "having truly entered into the Bodhisattva vehicle."Focusing on the absence of those who do not possess the oral instructions, he says, "Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata obtain any phenomenon whatsoever from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara?" and so on, elaborating: "Subhūti, if the Tathāgata had obtained any phenomenon whatsoever from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara that is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete, then he would not have been predicted."What is the intention of this? It is to say: "If there were a phenomenon to be realized that could be obtained, then I would have attained perfect and complete buddhahood just as the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara attained it."Furthermore, he speaks at length, saying, "If the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had not predicted it..." Therefore, because there is no phenomenon that is actually obtained, he attained perfect and complete buddhahood beyond that limit; thus, it should be understood that the intention here is the statement, "Therefore, I was predicted."Why is it said that there is no phenomenon that is actually obtained? Subhūti, it is said that what is called a Tathāgata is the true suchness. Regarding that, the synonym for suchness is the Tathāgata, who is distinguished by perfect purity; the intention is that suchness itself is also not obtained. Regarding the expression of perfectly pure suchness and true suchness, the "true" is like gold.In order to abandon the grasping that "I have not fully awakened to any phenomenon from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, but I, the Blessed One, have fully awakened later," he speaks at length, saying, "Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."Subhūti, the statement that "the phenomena to which the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened are neither true nor false" clearly demonstrates the non-duality of suchness. How is it not true? It is because there is nothing to be obtained. How is it not false? It is because of the way in which perfect and complete buddhahood is attained; for in that, there is no occurrence of anything being actually obtained.Therefore, what is the intention behind the Tathāgata’s statement that "all phenomena are the qualities of a buddha"? It is because the qualities of a buddha are distinguished by the perfect purity of suchness, and the intention of this statement is that all phenomena follow after suchness.Because of the ultimate establishment that "all phenomena are not established as phenomena," it is said, "Subhūti, what are called 'all phenomena' are all devoid of phenomena; therefore, they are called 'the qualities of a buddha.'"In terms of realization, the statement, "Subhūti, it is as if a person were endowed with a human body and had become a great body," is explained extensively. This clearly demonstrates the attainment of the gnosis of realization and the absence of the pride of realization. How is the gnosis attained? It is by taking up two types of gnosis: the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage and the gnosis of equality. The gnosis by which one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, becoming definitively established in the lineage of a buddha, is the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage; by attaining this, one becomes endowed with a body.
