This refers to that which causes one to rejoice for many lifetimes; one who has been born into the lineage becomes endowed with a body, and therefore it is called "endowed with a body." The gnosis of equality is also taken up by way of five types of equality: the equality of the latent propensity for defilement, the equality of selflessness, the equality of diligence in abandonment, the equality of diligence in a mind free from attachment, and the equality of the realization of all bodhisattvas. By hearing these, one becomes a "great body," because one takes up the bodies of all sentient beings. That body of his is neither his own nor another's, yet he is able to abide in it.Therefore, the statement by the Tathāgata, "a person endowed with a human body and a great body," is explained extensively by the Tathāgata as "not having a body," and so on. Regarding this, "endowed with a body" and "great body" establish the mode of ultimate reality here, which is, for the time being, through the attainment of gnosis.If one asks how there is no conceit, it is because of what is stated extensively: "Any bodhisattva who says thus..." What does this clarify? If one thinks, "I shall lead sentient beings to complete nirvana," that bodhisattva should be known as having conceit; in the ultimate sense, they are not to be called a "bodhisattva."Therefore, if one asks what is clarified by the Tathāgata’s statement that "all phenomena are without sentient beings," it is this: if sentient beings truly existed, how could a bodhisattva be endowed with a body and a great body in that way?Prior to this, based on the search for the buddha-bhūmi and the perfection of the purity of the buddha-kṣetra, it is stated: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva says, 'I shall accomplish the arrays of the buddha-kṣetra,' that too should be spoken of in the same way." This is the meaning of saying, "They are not to be called a 'bodhisattva.'"Having a view regarding that leads to engagement in authentic practice; therefore, in order to abandon that, one establishes the ultimate meaning, for the Tathāgata has stated that those are without arrays; thus, it is said, "the arrays of the buddha-kṣetra.""Subhūti, any bodhisattva who has the conviction that 'phenomena are selfless, phenomena are selfless'" is stated with regard to the two types of selflessness: the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. The statement, "The Tathāgata calls them a 'bodhisattva', a 'bodhisattva'," is made with regard to the two types of perfect awakening to those very two types of selflessness. If one asks what this clarifies, it is that the grasping at a person as "I shall accomplish" and the grasping at phenomena as "the arrays of the buddha-kṣetra" do not exist in those bodhisattvas.Based on the perfection of unsurpassed vision and primordial wisdom, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?" In order to make it known that the Tathāgata possesses supreme and perfectly pure vision, it is shown that he does not possess only the eye of prajñāpāramitā, but that he possesses the five types of eyes. Otherwise, one would seek perfectly pure vision only through the eye of prajñāpāramitā. In summary, there are four types of eyes: the one that perceives form, the one that perceives the ultimate truth, the one that perceives conventional truth, and the one that perceives all knowable things in every aspect. The one that perceives form is also of two types: the result of karma and the result of meditation. Therefore, there are five types. The first is the perception of form due to having a vast object. Because of knowing the ultimate, one engages in knowing the conventional without error; therefore, the perception of the ultimate truth is the former. Regarding that, what is expressed as phenomena and persons is what is designated as phenomena and persons. Knowing those is called the eye of Dharma; this is the perfectly pure vision of the extent of all things.The statement, "I fully know the continuum of minds of those various beings with their diverse intentions," refers to perfectly pure primordial wisdom. Regarding that, the continuum of minds refers to the minds of the three times. Regarding that, diverse intentions should be understood as being of two types: afflicted and purified, or what is called "with attachment" and "without attachment," and so forth. Alternatively, it is by the division of past and so forth.In this way, both are established in terms of ultimate reality; the statement "the continuum of mind is no continuum" and the statement "the past mind is also not to be apprehended" are taught extensively. Regarding that, the past mind is not to be apprehended because it has subsided. The future mind is not to be apprehended because it has not arisen. The present mind is ultimate reality, and it is established as a vision based upon the nature of the object of knowledge that is directly perceived. Then, there is the primordial wisdom that is based upon teaching the intentions of sentient beings just as they are; this is what is meant by the statement, "Here, the continuum of mind is no continuum." If one asks why it was not similarly stated, "Regarding the perfectly pure vision, the eye is no eye," it is because the primordial wisdom and the perfectly pure vision are a single basis, and because what is established as the ultimate, final reality is established from the very beginning.Having focused on the perfection of the mass of merit that has become sovereign, it is taught extensively, "By which this great trichiliocosm world system..."Here too, it is established in terms of ultimate reality; it is taught extensively, "Again, Subhūti, if there were a mass of merit..."Having focused on the perfection of the body and the perfection of the body’s secondary signs, it is taught extensively, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by the perfection of the form body?"Having focused on the perfection of the body’s marks, it is taught extensively, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by the perfection of the marks?"Having focused on the perfection of speech, it is taught extensively, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata think, 'I have taught the Dharma'?"Having focused on the perfection of the mind and the establishments of mindfulness, it is taught extensively, "Bhagavān, in the future time, whatever sentient beings hear this teaching of the Dharma, such as this..." This clarifies the intention of the Bhagavān regarding those sentient beings upon whom he has focused his mindfulness; that they are not sentient beings is from the perspective of the ultimate. That they are not without sentient beings is from the perspective of the conventional. That which is other than this is from the perspective of teaching the ultimate. The clarification of the meaning of the validity of those meanings that are uncommon is the same as before.Having focused on the perfection of the mind and the attainment of complete awakening, it is taught extensively, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata think that there is any Dharma whatsoever by which he has attained the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening?" Having completely abandoned the fault of the view that "there is no such Dharma," one seeks out awakening and the path to awakening; this is taught by means of two awakenings and two definitive expressions. This is by taking up the expression "unsurpassed" and the expression "perfectly," for the statement *anuttarāyāṃ samyaksambodhau dharmā na vidyante* takes up the expression *anuttarā* to reveal the own-nature of awakening. For that awakening, which has the nature of liberation, there is not even an atom of a conditioned phenomenon that arises; for that very reason, it is not an object of apprehension. By that very fact, one should know that in the "subsequent" "Dharma" "existence," there is no existence.Furthermore, Subhūti, by the phrase *samāḥ sa dharmāḥ*, the expression "perfectly complete" is taken up to reveal the general characteristic of the person in relation to awakening; the statement "that Dharma is equal" refers to that by which one is designated as awakening and as a Buddha.By knowing that there is nothing whatsoever that is unequal in that regard, it is shown that all Buddhas, in the ultimate sense, are also without inequality regarding their life span and so forth.It is said that that unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening is equal by virtue of being without a life-principle.Revealing awakening from the general characteristic of the phenomena of cyclic existence, it is said: "By all wholesome phenomena, one is fully awakened." Revealing the path of awakening in its entirety, it is said: "Those are just so; those too are established by the characteristic of ultimate reality."With the intention of establishing the great meaning of the perfect mind, it is said extensively: "In the world system of the third-order great trichiliocosm, as many Mount Sumerus as there are," and so forth.With the intention of establishing the great meaning of the instruction, it is said extensively: "If you think, 'The Tathāgata thinks: I have liberated sentient beings,'" and so forth.What is the intention behind the statement that the Tathāgata would be grasping at a self? It should be viewed as follows: if the Tathāgata were to conceive of sentient beings because he knows the knowable exactly as it is, then the Tathāgata would be grasping at a self.In order to abandon the intense attachment of thinking that, although there is no self, there is for the time being a grasping at a self, it is said extensively: "Subhūti, the so-called 'grasping at a self' is a non-grasping."The statement that although childish ordinary beings grasp at it as existing, it does not exist to be grasped, is explained extensively by the phrase: "Subhūti, the so-called 'childish ordinary beings' are those who are not beings," and those are just so.With regard to the perfect excellence of the mind, which is the Dharmakāya, it is said extensively: "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be viewed by means of the perfect excellence of marks?" The first verse clearly demonstrates how one does not see and by whom one does not see. If one asks how one does not see, it is by means of conventions such as "view." What is called "abandoning" is meditative absorption; whoever is a practitioner of meditative absorption is called one who abandons, and that consists of both reflection and cultivation. Through reflection, one grasps at what is not that, and through cultivation, one cognizes incorrectly; it should be understood that by engaging in abandoning, one grasps at the convention of incorrect cognition. If one asks by whom one does not see, it is by those beings who are engaged in conventions.The first half of the second verse clearly demonstrates what is not seen, and the latter half demonstrates the cause by which one does not see. Regarding that, the statement "The Buddhas see the Dharmatā" is intended to mean that this phenomenon is the meaning of the Tathāgata.Regarding the cause by which one knows, it is said: "The Guides are the Dharmakāya." Because the Buddhas, who are all-pervading and focused on suchness, are the pure body, they should be viewed as Dharmatā; this is how one views them. If one asks again, by what cause are they not to be viewed? Because the Dharmatā, which is the characteristic of suchness, cannot be cognized by literal interpretation, and because it must be realized by each individual for themselves, it is said that one cannot cognize it through non-literal interpretation either, as one does not see it. The statement that clearly demonstrates this meaning is: "Since Dharmatā cannot be cognized, it cannot be cognized by that." Similarly, here, the fact that the basis of the Dharmakāya is not to be viewed as the Tathāgata is demonstrated by the statement "not by the perfect excellence of marks," meaning that the perfect excellence of marks is not to be viewed as the Tathāgata.In order to abandon the mental attachment of thinking that one has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment due to the cause of the perfect excellence of marks, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? Do you hold that the Tathāgata has manifestly and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfect excellence of marks?" Regarding those, it is like that.With regard to the perfect excellence of the mind not abiding in either cyclic existence or nirvāṇa, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, do you think that those who have truly entered into the vehicle of the bodhisattvas..." In this regard, that there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is designated as being destroyed is the Dharmatā as it abides. That there is no cessation is due to individual realization; because the phenomena of cyclic existence have become subject to one's control, like reflections and emanations, one again engages thoroughly for the benefit of sentient beings. By this, the truth of the one who travels only to peace is temporarily refuted, thereby clearly demonstrating the state of not abiding in nirvāṇa.Then, in order to not abide in nirvāṇa and to completely abandon the association with the defilements of cyclic existence, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, a son or daughter of noble family..." Regarding the meaning of "those phenomena that are selfless and unborn," what is it? That which the Tathāgata has mastered, whose engagement is of the nature of an emanation, is not the nature of the phenomena of cyclic existence, nor does it arise from karma and defilements; that which has become subject to one's control is called "selfless and unborn." What is the reason for understanding this? Otherwise, if one were not to become defiled in cyclic existence by merely holding onto the merit as described, then what need is there to mention bodhisattvas who have patience in the selfless and unborn? For by attaining patience in the unborn, an immense amount of merit will arise.Again, Subhūti, the statement "a bodhisattva should not grasp at a mass of merit" clearly demonstrates the state of not abiding in cyclic existence; for by not abiding in cyclic existence, one grasps at a mass of merit.The Venerable Subhūti asked, "What is the intention behind the statement 'one should not grasp at a mass of merit'? For the Bhagavan has elsewhere stated that one should grasp at a mass of merit."The Bhagavan replied, "Although one should grasp at it, one should not grasp at it wrongly; thus, by way of this distinction, it is taught that it should be grasped. How one should not grasp at it wrongly is just as previously explained; it is those very points."With regard to the physical postures of movement and abiding, which are the perfection of the mind, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, if someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata comes or goes...'" In this context, movement refers to walking, and abiding refers to standing. The remainder refers to the physical postures.With regard to the movement and abiding that are mastered through the meditation on the body of form and name, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, if a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family were to take as many atoms of earth as there are in the great trichiliocosm..." In this case, there is a method for making things subtle and a method for making things appear non-existent; one should understand that meditating on this is just as previously explained. The question, "Do you think that the collection of those atoms is numerous?" refers here to "as many as there are," which is the method for making things subtle."Bhagavan, if there were a collection, the Bhagavan would not have spoken of a 'collection of atoms'—this and similar statements are methods for making things appear non-existent. Why is it explained in that way? If a collection of atoms existed in the ultimate sense, the Bhagavan would not have said that those collections do not exist."It is explained in that way because the Bhagavan stated that those collections of atoms are not collections.If one asks why it is stated again, even though it was previously explained that what is called a "collection of atoms" is not established as having the nature of a collection, and even though it leads to the idea of a collection: it is because the Tathāgata stated that those elements do not exist, which is the very method for making things appear non-existent; one should understand that meditating on the body of names is just as previously explained. Here, the "world of the three realms" refers to the world of sentient beings, which is also differentiated by collections of names."Bhagavan, if there were a world-system, it would be an apprehension of a whole"—this statement was spoken by taking as the object both what the world-system is and what an atom is. Apprehension of a whole is of two types: apprehension of a whole as a unity, and apprehension of a whole by way of analysis. Regarding these, the existence of a world-system is an apprehension of a whole as a unity, such as thinking "a sentient being" in relation to the aggregates; and the existence of an atom is an apprehension of a whole by way of analysis, for it is an apprehension of a whole by grasping at a collection of atoms.Here, the term "apprehension" is also established in the ultimate sense by the noble Subhūti, and the Bhagavan confirms that very meaning by stating at length that "apprehension of a whole is merely a convention." How is this known? It is known through convention.That apprehension of a whole is also, in the ultimate sense, inexpressible. It is said that what is grasped by ordinary childish beings is merely according to worldly convention, and not in the ultimate sense. Having explained the meditation on the method for making appearances non-existent, [the text] also establishes the yoga and meditative equipoise that make appearances non-existent; and that which is called "non-conceptualizing" is precisely non-conceptualizing as it is.That which teaches what is not conceptualized, by whom, and in what way, prior to that, is the passage beginning with, "Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has spoken of a view of a self," and so forth, which is explained at length. By this, the way in which one does not conceptualize is clearly demonstrated.How is this so? The assertion of a self by other, non-Buddhist schools, and the Tathāgata’s speaking of a self, are both established as the selflessness of the person. That the view of a self is also spoken of as having no view establishes the selflessness of phenomena. If one engages in such a practice—where there is no apprehension of a view regarding that view of a self—one will enter into meditative equipoise; thus, that non-conceptualization is the method for entering into it.Subhūti, the phrase "entering correctly into the vehicle of the Bodhisattva" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptualization. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that upon which one is to engage in non-conceptualization. The phrase "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" begins from the higher mind and higher wisdom; by means of knowing, seeing, and resolving, it indicates by what means one is to engage in non-conceptualization. In this regard, that which relies on śamatha is prajñā. That which relies on vipaśyanā is jñāna. Both seeing and knowing are here the samādhi of resolution, and by the power of samādhi, one resolves intensely upon the object as if it were a reflection.The phrase "one should resolve in such a way that one does not abide even in the perception of phenomena" fully demonstrates what the conceptualization is, and those are precisely it. The "perception of phenomena" indicates the meaning of the logic of the uncommon; this is the method for entering into meditative equipoise, and it should be understood as the basis for everything. One should engage only to the extent of cutting off aspiration, prayer, and distraction. Therefore, the method has been explained by those points, and it is exactly like that.In order to demonstrate the perfection of the mind, and having taken as the basis the absence of defilement, it is further stated at length: "Subhūti, by what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..." What does this demonstrate? Because this Dharma possesses great meaning, it must undoubtedly be clarified correctly. Nevertheless, it must be clarified in such a way that it does not become a source of defilement.What is the intention behind saying, "How does one correctly demonstrate? It is by demonstrating in such a way that one does not demonstrate at all; therefore, it is called correctly demonstrating"? It means that the Dharma, which is of the nature of being inexpressible, cannot be demonstrated. Otherwise, it would be demonstrated through affliction, and because that meaning is erroneous, there is no supreme clarity or aspiration toward such a demonstration.
